newsitem.title: FINLAND: Summit notebook - Walking stick or telescope?.
newsitem.headline: Summit notebook - Walking stick or telescope?.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, clear winner in the public relations stakes ahead of his summit with Bill Clinton, seemed to score again in the post-summit gifts.
He gave the wheelchair-bound U.S. president an ornate walking stick in three pieces, U.S. officials said. But there was a telescope at one end of it.
Clinton's gift to Yeltsin was a replica sculpture showing an Indian riding down a mountainside, which officials said Clinton saw symbolising the Kremlin chief's political survival skills.
Loud nocturnal banging on Clinton's hotel room ceiling disturbed him on the eve of the summit, and he said he speculated briefly on Russian sabotage.
"Boris, I thought you had hired an extra-large Finn to stomp on my roof," White House spokesman Mike McCurry quoted Clinton as telling Yeltsin as they started their meeting.
There was also talk of a problem with the hotel sauna pipes but U.S. officials subsequently retracted this.
While the presidents dined in a spirit of peace on Thursday evening and got ready to discuss arms control, Helsinki-dwellers had a sneak preview of the latest Star Wars film.
Distributor Finnkino said the premiere date was set well ahead of the two-day summit, but the preview for nearly 700 Finns was "a happy coincidence".

Summit protocol meant carting a load of white gilt-rimmed official U.S. crockery to Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari's official residence, Mantyniemi, where the United States was hosting Friday's lunch.
Ahtisaari hosted Thursday evening's supper. President Boris Yeltsin hosted a supper before President Bill Clinton headed back to Washington on Friday.

Internet summiteers said thousands worldwide visited their video and audio sites showing the presidents' arrivals on Thursday. State broadcaster YLE said its home page had a "colossal" 55,000 "hits" or visits, with 3,300 at its video site. A4 Media reported 6,500 "hits" for its web camera.
Both sites can be reached through http://virtual.finland.fi.
Finnish designer Marja Kurki who gave U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright a "busy bee" bright red scarf, was delighted to see her wearing it on Thursday.
